```{python}
    p.drop("MIKE", (3.0, 2.6), speed=3.0); p.drop("SAM", (3.0, 7.4), speed=3.0)
    p.highlight("FS", "Z")
    return p


boot = boot_play()
fld = clip(boot.draw(lateral=(-25, 14), window=(-9.5, 24.5), title=False))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, boot)
say(fld, boot, "FS: U's fake block says run,\nso he steps up; the over\nroute lands behind him", (18.4, 0.5), fs=6.3)
say(fld, boot, "CB: MOD, carries X", (22.6, -14.6), fs=6.3)
say(fld, boot, "deep", (16.0, -18.4), fs=6.0, color=style.OFFENSE)
say(fld, boot, "~12 yd", (15.4, -12.4), fs=6.0, color=style.OFFENSE)
say(fld, boot, "flat", (4.8, -12.6), fs=6.0, color=style.OFFENSE)
say(fld, boot, "U: fakes a\nblock, then\nleaks out", (-4.0, -10.8), fs=6.0)
say(fld, boot, "trailing CB", (14.6, -2.2), fs=6.0)
plt.show()
```

Walk through it from the defense's side. The corner saw #1 go deep and went with him: correct,
MOD. The Will saw a run fake, stepped up, then chased U to the flat: correct. The free safety read
#2, saw a block and came forward: correct by his rule, and wrong, because U's block was a fake. An
honest pass never fools a quarters safety, since #2 running a route is the clearest pass read
there is; a pass dressed as a run can, because for a beat the fake and the real thing look the
same. The over route, coming from the other side of the field, entered the space between the
corner (deep with X) and the safety (up for the run) where *nobody's rule* put a defender: three
receivers at three depths on one side, against defenders whose first read sent them the wrong way.
The fake has to hold one more defender. On a bootleg the end on the side the quarterback rolls to
is usually left unblocked, so the quarterback is running toward a free rusher who must bite on the
run fake too.

It isn't that play-action is magic against quarters in particular. In the nflverse charting for
2023–2025, play-action raised the average result of a dropback against quarters by about as much
as it did against Cover 3 or Cover 1.[^pa] The point is *which* play-action. A run fake that pulls
the safeties forward, paired with a deep crosser from the far side, attacks the exact gap between
quarters' corner rule and its safety rule. The defense's counter is discipline in the read (safeties
taught to key through the blocker to the linemen and the quarterback, not just #2's first step) and
calls that tell the safety on the bootleg side to stay deep no matter what, at the cost of the run
fit.

### The running back's wheel

The third weakness hides in the rule for the apex defender: *take the first man to the flat.*

```{python}
#| label: fig-rb-wheel
#| fig-cap: "The running back's wheel against quarters, offense's right side. Z (#1) runs a dig, past 5 yards, so it counts as deep and the corner (MOD) stays on him and follows him inside. Y (#2) runs a quick slant inside, so the strong safety, with no vertical #2, works inside and over the top to bracket Z's dig, and the Mike takes the slant. The running back (R, ringed, aligned to the quarterback's right) releases to the flat; the nickel ($, ringed) takes him as the first man to the flat, and then the back turns up the sideline. The ball is caught about 15 yards downfield with the nickel chasing from behind and the deep outside quarter empty: the corner and the safety both went inside with the routes in front of them."
off = [q.moved(w=2.3) if q.key == "RB" else q for q in spread_2x2()]   # back offset to the QB's right
p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, {"NB": (4.8, 6.2), "WILL": (4.8, -2.4), "MIKE": (4.8, 1.6)}), los=35, to_go=None)
p.zone((19.0, 20.5), (8.0, 9.0), "empty")
p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 12)); p.route("Y", r.slant(2, 6))
p.route("RB", [(-3.8, 8.0), (-1.2, 12.6), (2.0, 17.6), (8.0, 20.2), (20.0, 20.8)], absolute=True, speed=7.5)
p.dropback(2.5); p.pass_to("RB", t=2.2)
protect(p)
p.drop("RCB", (10.6, 14.6), speed=5.0); p.drop("RCB", (11.8, 10.2), speed=5.0)   # MOD: #1 went deep, stay on him
p.drop("SS", (13.6, 7.6), speed=4.0)                                          # #2 not vertical: bracket #1
p.drop("MIKE", (5.6, 4.0), speed=4.0); p.drop("WILL", (6.5, -2.0))
p.drop("NB", (5.4, 8.0), speed=3.0); p.drop("NB", (2.5, 12.5), speed=5.0)     # first man to the flat...
p.drop("NB", (4.0, 16.8), speed=5.0); p.drop("NB", (10.6, 19.0), speed=5.0)                                         # ...then chasing up the sideline
p.highlight("NB", "RB")
fld = clip(p.draw(lateral=(-5, 26.6), window=(-8.5, 25.0), title=False))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p)
say(fld, p, "SS: #2 not vertical,\nso bracket #1's dig", (16.8, 7.0), fs=6.3)
say(fld, p, "CB: dig > 5 yd,\nMOD stays on #1", (6.6, 10.6), fs=6.3)
say(fld, p, "$: first man to the flat,\nnow chasing from behind", (-5.0, 18.4), fs=6.3)
plt.show()
```

Each rule is reasonable on its own. Together, the routes in front of the corner and the safety
pulled both of them inside, and the back's route started as a flat route (the apex defender's) and
became a deep route down the sideline (nobody's). The defender left with him is a nickel back or a
linebacker, chasing a running back from behind, with an empty deep quarter in front of them. The
wheel is the classic match-coverage beater because it *changes category* in the middle of the play:
short when the rules assign it, deep when it's caught.

Defenses answer by teaching the apex player to "carry" a flat route that turns up, and by telling
the corner, when #1 goes inside, to look for something coming outside behind him; each answer
loosens something else. The offense's side of all this, the full menu of concepts aimed at
quarters' rules, is the job of
[Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd).

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Rams 2020 — the two-high shell and its quarters share"}
Brandon Staley's one season as the Rams' defensive coordinator is usually told as a story about
disguise ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)
tells it that way). Underneath the disguise was a lot of plain quarters. In the nflverse charting
for the 2020 regular season, the Rams played quarters or Cover 6 on 36.1% of charted dropbacks,
third-most in the league behind San Francisco and Chicago, against a league rate of 20.4%. Their
single most common coverage after the snap was still Cover 3 (41.8%), much of it rotated down from
a two-high look; quarters and Cover 6 were the next biggest pieces.[^rams] Staley had come from
Fangio's staffs in Chicago and Denver, and the Rams had the two players a quarters defense most
wants: Aaron Donald, an interior pass rusher who could win with four, and Jalen Ramsey, a
cornerback who could play outside or in the slot.[^staley]

**What to notice:** on a Rams early down from 2020, check the safeties' depth before the snap.
They are often at 10 yards or less, over the slot or the tight end, not at 13 on the hashes. Then
watch the first step of the safety on the tight end's side. On runs he comes downhill into the
alley; on passes with the tight end releasing, he turns and runs with him. Expect rotation on many
snaps too: a safety who spins into the deep middle at the snap isn't a contradiction, just the
Cover 3 half of the menu.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Broncos 2022 — Ejiro Evero and the trusted corner"}
Ejiro Evero, a safeties and secondary coach on the Rams' staff through 2021, became Denver's
defensive coordinator in 2022. The Broncos went 5–12 that season, but not because of the defense:
it finished seventh in the NFL in total defense (320 yards a game) and tied for third in net yards
per pass attempt (5.6).[^broncos] In the nflverse charting the 2022 Broncos played quarters or
Cover 6 on 33.3% of dropbacks, sixth in the league (the league rate was 24.8%), though, as with the
Rams, Cover 3 was their most common single coverage (46.8%). Their second-year cornerback Patrick
Surtain II was named first-team All-Pro.[^surtain] Evero has run Carolina's defense since 2023 and
returns as its coordinator in 2026.

**What to notice:** this is the place to watch the corner rules. A corner the defense trusts alone
lets it play MEG on one side and lean its safety toward the other, or bracket the other side's best
receiver in Cover 6. On a 2022 Broncos passing down, find Surtain first, then the safety on his
side. If the safety drifts away from him at the snap, Surtain is likely on an island by design.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Michigan State 2013 — Narduzzi's quarters"}
The college reference point. Michigan State's 2013 defense, coordinated by Pat Narduzzi, led the
nation in total defense through the regular season (248.2 yards a game) and ranked third in scoring
defense (11.3 points a game), and Narduzzi won the Broyles Award as the top assistant in college
football.[^msu2013] Cornerback Darqueze Dennard won the Thorpe Award as the nation's best defensive
back, the first Spartan to win it.[^dennard] The defense was a 4-3 with quarters behind it: two
safeties at 8 to 10 yards reading #2 and fitting the run, and corners who played their receivers
aggressively, so aggressively that Narduzzi admitted his quarters "can look like man a lot of the
time."[^narduzzi-man]

**What to notice:** if you find 2013 Michigan State film, count the run defenders on a running
play one second after the snap. Seven start near the line; within a second there are often nine,
as both safeties arrive. On passes, watch the corners press and carry receivers deep: MOD from
press, which is why it looks like man.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: two-high, now what?"}
When the defense shows two deep safeties, don't stop at "two-high." Use the next three looks. On
the broadcast angle the safeties are usually in the frame before the snap and the wide corners
often aren't, so read the safeties live and save the corners for the replay.

- **Before the snap: depth and width.** Safeties at 12 to 14 yards, outside the hashes: think Cover 2
  or a half-field player. Safeties at 8 to 10 yards over the slot or the tight end: think quarters.
  One deep and wide, one shallow and inside: think Cover 6, with the half on the deep safety's side.
  Then the corners, if you can see them: both off 7 or 8 yards, eyes on their receivers, suggests
  quarters; one squatting at 5 with outside leverage suggests a Cover 2 half; one a yard or two
  shallower than the other, with his shoulders turned in to the slot, suggests Palms.
- **At the snap: the safeties' first steps.** Watch one safety for one second. *Backpedal* or turn
  and run for the sideline: a half-field player (Cover 2, or the Cover 2 side of Cover 6). *Downhill*
  toward the line: a quarters safety reading run, or a called rotation (the other safety will tell
  you which: if he runs to the middle, it's a rotation to one-high). *Flat-footed, then with #2 up
  the seam*: quarters, carrying #2.
- **One second later: the corners.** Both bailing with eyes on the quarterback: quarters. Both
  squatting: Cover 2. One of each: Cover 6. A corner coming *forward* toward the slot's out route
  while the safety on that side runs deep and wide over the outside receiver: Palms.
- **Then watch the ball.** On runs, find the first defender to the ball. If it's a safety arriving
  three to five yards downfield, you've just watched quarters' run fit. On passes, note whether the
  completion was short and outside (what quarters concedes) or deep (what it exists to stop).
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the shallow safeties"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-shallow
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-12 from the offense's 40. 11 personnel, 2x2, tight end attached on the right. The two safeties are ringed. Read their depth from the numbers on the left and their width from the hash marks along the bottom, then look at the corners and count the box."
off = pro_2x2()
pr1 = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, {"FS": (9.0, -7.0), "SS": (9.0, 6.6)}), los=40, to_go=12)
pr1.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = pr1.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 16.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr1, widths=True)
plt.show()
```

**What coverage family is this most likely to be, and if you were calling plays, which run and
which pass would you like against it on second-and-12?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Quarters, or something that will look like it for a beat.** Two safeties at 9 yards, inside the
slot on the left and just outside the tight end on the right, are reading safeties, not half-field
players: a Cover 2 safety would be at 12 to 14 and outside the hash, because he has to reach the
sideline. Off corners on both sides fit quarters' MOD rule. Six defenders in the box against six
blockers is the quarters light box. (A defense can still rotate out of this at the snap, as
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd) shows.)

**The situation matters.** On second-and-12 the defense is happy to give up a four-yard run or a
five-yard out and keep everything in front of it; that leaves third-and-long. The offense wants a
chunk, so attack the safety's read rather than take what quarters concedes.

**The run:** if you run, run *away* from the tight end, toward the slot side, and have H release up
the field so the free safety has to go with him; that takes one fitter out. Or call an RPO that
reads that safety: hand off if he stays deep, throw behind him if he comes down.

**The pass:** play-action with a deep crosser (the safeties step up on the run fake), or a route
combination that makes the safety and corner cross, such as scissors. The quick out by #2 is there
too, unless the corner is playing Palms, but on second-and-12 it only gets you to third-and-7. Four
verticals is the one call this defense was built for.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the halves disagree"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-cover6
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-11. Trips to the offense's right (Z, H and the attached tight end Y), X alone on the left. Two-high. Compare the two halves of the defense: the three ringed defenders are the ones to read, using the depth numbers and the hash marks."
off = offense("gun_trips")
mv = {"RCB": (7.5, 17.6), "SS": (9.5, 8.6), "NB": (4.6, 7.5), "MIKE": (4.8, 2.4), "WILL": (4.8, -2.2),
      "LCB": (5.0, -16.3), "FS": (13.0, -7.0)}
pr2 = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, mv), los=45, to_go=11)
pr2.highlight("LCB", "FS", "RCB")
fld = pr2.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 17.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr2, widths=True)
plt.show()
```

**What is the coverage likely to be? The offense's best receiver is X. Should the quarterback
throw to him?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Most likely Cover 6, with the Cover 2 half on X.** The left side is a Cover 2 picture: a squat
corner (5 yards, outside leverage, ready to take the flat and the quick out) and a deep safety, 13
yards and outside the hash, who can reach the sideline over the top. The right side is a quarters
picture: an off corner and a shallower safety inside #2. Two halves, two coverages.

**Probably not to X.** The offense put its best receiver alone to get him one-on-one, and Cover 6 is
built to deny exactly that: X has a corner underneath and a safety over the top. On third-and-11 a
hitch or quick out is short of the sticks *and* runs into the squat corner; a go route runs into
the half-field safety. The one window on that side is the Cover 2 hole shot, the sideline between
the corner and the safety, 18 to 22 yards deep, and it needs a perfect throw.

**Throw to the trips side instead,** where four defenders cover three receivers and the routes can
get past 11 yards. The pressure point is #3: send the tight end straight up the middle with H up
the seam beside him. The strong safety takes H, and the Mike is left running down the field with
the tight end.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-2, the quick out is called"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-palms
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-2 from the offense's 30. The play call: H (#2) runs a quick out at 4 yards, the classic conversion throw, and X (#1) runs a go route to clear the corner out (both routes drawn). The defense shows two-high. Compare the two ringed corners: the right one is square to Z, eyes on him; the left one's shoulders are turned in toward H. Check their depths too."
off = spread_2x2()
pr3 = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, {"LCB": (6.3, -15.9)}), los=30, to_go=2)
pr3.route("H", r.out(4, 6)); pr3.route("X", r.go(14))
pr3.highlight("LCB", "RCB")
fld = pr3.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 17.0))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr3, widths=True)
say(fld, pr3, "#1", (-4.0, -15.0), fs=6.6); say(fld, pr3, "#2", (-4.8, -9.0), fs=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**The quarterback sees an off corner and thinks the quick out to H is free. What is the danger,
and what would you call the next time you see this corner?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The danger is Palms: the trap.** The left corner is a yard or so shallower than the right one,
square to X but turned in toward the slot: he is reading #2. When H breaks out, the corner leaves X
and drives forward, outside-in, onto the out, and the free safety, seeing #2 go out, takes X deep.
X's go route was supposed to clear the corner away; instead it runs into the safety, and the quick
out is thrown into a defender coming downhill. The situation is part of the tell: on third-and-2
the quick out to #2 is the obvious conversion throw, which is exactly when a defense calls the
trap. Best case for the offense, an incompletion and a punt; worst case, an interception returned
the other way.

**Next time, bait the trap.** Call an out-and-up for H (or a wheel): the same first 4 yards, then
up the sideline behind the jumping corner, with the safety busy with X. Or attack the moment the
corner looks inside: a quick slant by X, breaking inside a corner whose eyes are on H. The deeper
lesson is the trade every match rule makes. Palms takes away the quick out, and in doing so tells
you which route will beat it.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Quarters is a read coverage, not four deep zones.** Corners and safeties start with deep
  quarters, but the receivers' releases decide who covers whom: the corner takes #1 deep (MOD), the
  safety reads #2. It is the purest pattern-matching coverage in common use.
- **The read safety is the whole design.** One key, #2, gives three answers: carry him if he goes
  vertical, bracket #1 if he goes out or short, fill the alley if he blocks. Standing 8 to 10 yards
  deep lets one player be a deep defender and a run defender on the same snap.
- **MOD and MEG are a trade between help and freedom.** MOD lets short routes go to the underneath
  defenders and doubles the deep ones; MEG locks a trusted corner on his man and frees a teammate
  for another job.
- **Cover 6 and Palms fix quarters' soft spots without adding a player.** Cover 6 puts a Cover 2
  half on the lone receiver (under-over on him) and quarters on the trips side; Palms swaps the
  corner and safety so the corner can trap #2's quick out.
- **Two-high match spread because it stops explosive passes without surrendering the run, answers
  spread passing concepts, and disguises well.** Split-safety coverage rose from 32.9% of dropbacks
  in 2018 to 42.0% in 2025 by NGS's count; the charting data agree on the total but split it
  differently across the 2022/2023 source break.
- **Its holes follow from its rules:** light-box runs when receivers take the safeties away, the
  bootleg flood that turns the safeties' run read against them, and the wheel that changes from a
  flat route to a deep one after the rules have assigned it.

corner that Cover 6 borrows), and [Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)

**Sets up:** [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd),
which starts from the two-high shell built here and shows how it changes at the snap, the trips
checks (poach and its cousins) and Saban's Cover 7; [Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd),
the offense's menu against quarters; [The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd),
where split-field quarters grew up against the spread; [The Modern Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd),
on the two-high wave and the offenses' heavy-personnel answer; and
[Tendencies, PROE and Charting](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd),
which works with the coverage labels charted above.

**Case study:** [Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)
follows the two-high family through the NFL's most influential two-high coordinator and the defense
built to beat the offenses that adapted to it.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- Cody Alexander, *Match Quarters: A Modern Guidebook to Split-Field Coverages*, and his MatchQuarters
  newsletter: the most thorough public treatment of quarters, Cover 6 and Palms from a coach's point
  of view.
- Cameron Soran, "The Complete Guide to Nick Saban Coverages at Alabama," Throw Deep Publishing
  (2021): MOD, MEG, Palms, Stubbie and Cover 7, rule by rule.
- Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015) and his Grantland piece on Gary Patterson's TCU
  defense: the best short introductions to why quarters took over college football.
- X&O Labs' clinic-style reports on two-high coverage structures, and Pat Narduzzi's Cover 4 clinic
  talks, for the run-fit side.
:::

[^patterson]: Chris B. Brown, "Hard Knocks: Playing Defense With TCU's Gary Patterson," Grantland (Sept. 1, 2015): https://grantland.com/features/hard-knocks-playing-defense-with-tcus-gary-patterson/ ("Other teams have their safeties backpedal, but we sit there and flat-foot shuffle," Patterson at a 2015 clinic).

[^soran-mod]: Cameron Soran, "The Complete Guide to Nick Saban Coverages at Alabama," Throw Deep Publishing (Feb. 24, 2021): https://throwdeeppublishing.com/blogs/news/nick-saban-s-alabama-pass-coverages . MOD: "The corner will be man-to-man on all #1 except when #1 breaks at 5 yards or less (e.g., shallow cross, 5 yard hitch). If #1 breaks at 5 yards or less, zone to deep quarter." Safety: "Take all of #2 vertical. If #2 is not vertical, then bracket #1." Apex: "Take the first man to the flat... If #2 begins to go vertical, always reroute #2." MEG: "Man Everywhere he Goes... the corner will man up on #1 for everything (no exceptions)." In Saban's version the MOD corner begins in press; most quarters teams play it from off alignments.

[^ngs]: James Reber, NFL Next Gen Stats, "The coverage that turned the Seahawks into Super Bowl winners and is taking the NFL by storm," NFL.com (2026): https://www.nfl.com/news/the-coverage-that-turned-the-seahawks-into-super-bowl-winners-and-is-taking-the-nfl-by-storm (2025 coverage rates: Cover 4 17.2%, Cover 2 13.9%, Cover 6 9.2%).

[^soran-palms]: Soran's guide, cited in full in the note on MOD and MEG: Palms, strong safety: "Take #1 vertical if #2 is out in first 5 yards. Otherwise, take all of #2 vertical. If #2 is not vertical, then bracket #1." The names vary by staff. "Palms," "2-read" and "2 Trap" are the common ones; Alex Kirby, "2 Read Coverage: One Coverage that Solves a TON of Problems," Throw Deep Publishing (June 8, 2021): https://throwdeeppublishing.com/blogs/news/one-coverage-that-solves-a-ton-of-problems , notes that Dave Aranda's playbook calls it "Nail," and some playbooks use "Palms" for a broader family. Corner alignment and the man-on-#1 rule when #2 is vertical follow common 2-read teaching; details differ by staff.

[^ngs-detail]: Same NFL.com Next Gen Stats article as the note on Cover 6 (split-safety rate 32.9% in 2018, 37.8% in 2021, 40.4% in 2024, 42.0% in 2025; every defense above 30% in 2025). The 2018–2024 Cover 4 average of 13.9% comes from the same Next Gen Stats analysis. A different series from TruMedia/538, measured on early downs only (26.8% in 2019 to 34.6% in 2024), circulates widely and should not be mixed with this one.

[^trend]: Course calculation from nflverse `load_participation()`, 2018–2025 regular seasons (Weeks 1–17 through 2020, 1–18 from 2021), rows with a charted `defense_coverage_type`, excluding BLOWN, COMBO and PREVENT; two-high = COVER_2 + 2_MAN + COVER_4 + COVER_6 (COVER_9, which appears only from 2023, is counted as neither). Labels come from NGS for 2016–2022 and from FTN for 2023–2025, with different label sets, and none exist for 2016–2017. Small differences from other published nflverse calculations come from the filters.

[^2018]: "2018 Kansas City Chiefs–Los Angeles Rams game," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Kansas_City_Chiefs%E2%80%93Los_Angeles_Rams_game (Rams 54, Chiefs 51 on ESPN's Monday Night Football, Nov. 19, 2018, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum). Mahomes: CBS Sports, "2018 NFL MVP: Patrick Mahomes beats out Drew Brees for top award at NFL Honors" (Feb. 2019): https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/2018-nfl-mvp-patrick-mahomes-beats-out-drew-brees-for-top-award-at-nfl-honors/ (5,097 yards and 50 touchdown passes, the second player after Peyton Manning with 5,000 and 50).

[^cleveland]: Saban's pattern-matching Cover 3 "prior to his association with Belichick with the Browns in the early 1990s simply did not exist," in Cameron Soran's guide (cited in the note on MOD and MEG), which also treats Cover 7 as "a form of quarters coverage" and explains Rip/Liz as "the safety's declaration... of which side he is coming down." Dates: Kyle Jones, "Film Study: Nick Saban's Influence on Mark Dantonio and Ohio State's 2002 National Title Run Is Undeniable," Eleven Warriors (Mar. 23, 2020): https://elevenwarriors.com/ohio-state-football/film-study/2020/03/112969/film-study-nick-sabans-influence-on-mark-dantonio-and-ohio-states-2002-national-title-run-is-undeniable (Saban was Cleveland's defensive coordinator from 1991 to 1994, left for Michigan State in 1995 and hired Dantonio to coach the secondary).

[^narduzzi]: Zach Barnett, "How Ben Roethlisberger and Urban Meyer shaped Pat Narduzzi's defensive philosophy," FootballScoop (June 25, 2014): https://footballscoop.com/news/how-ben-roethlisberger-and-urban-meyer-shaped-pat-narduzzi-s-defensive-philosophy (Narduzzi was coaching linebackers at Northern Illinois in 2002; Roethlisberger went "41-of-61 passes for 525 yards with four touchdowns against three interceptions" in Northern Illinois's 48–41 win on Oct. 12, 2002; at Miami the next season, with Roethlisberger now on his own side, Narduzzi "hit Roethlisberger with a Cover 4," as he told an 80-minute Cover 4 talk at the Angelo Football Clinic).

[^msu2013]: Associated Press, "Michigan State's Narduzzi wins Broyles Award," *Arkansas Democrat-Gazette* (Dec. 10, 2013): https://www.arkansasonline.com/news/2013/dec/10/michigan-states-narduzzi-wins-broyles-award/ ("Michigan State leads the nation this season in total defense and third the nation in scoring defense, holding opponents to 248.2 yards and 11.3 points per game"; Narduzzi had been MSU's defensive coordinator since 2007). Final 2013 national rankings after the bowl games may differ slightly. Narduzzi left to become Pittsburgh's head coach in December 2014: Michigan State Athletics, "Pat Narduzzi Named Head Football Coach at Pittsburgh" (Dec. 26, 2014): https://msuspartans.com/news/2014/12/26/Pat_Narduzzi_Named_Head_Football_Coach_at_Pittsburgh .

[^iowa]: Phil Parker was named Iowa's defensive coordinator in February 2012, succeeding Norm Parker, who had run the defense since Kirk Ferentz's arrival: BTN.com staff, "Ferentz names Phil Parker DC, rearranges staff" (Feb. 7, 2012): https://btn.com/2012/02/07/ferentz-names-phil-parker-dc-rearranges-staff . On the scheme: Cody Alexander, "Fitting The Run With The Iowa Hawkeyes," MatchQuarters (June 13, 2024): https://www.matchquarters.com/p/fitting-the-run-iowa-hawkeyes-phil-parker-4-3 ("Phil Parker & Co. have taken the air out of their opponents' run games utilizing their Under 4-3 Quarters defense"). Norm Parker joined Ferentz's first staff before the 1999 season and was defensive coordinator through 2011: Hawkeye Sports, "Former Football Assistant Norm Parker Passes on Monday" (Jan. 13, 2014): https://hawkeyesports.com/news/2014/01/13/former-football-assistant-norm-parker-passes-on-monday .

[^pa]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play (regular-season dropbacks with EPA), joined to `load_participation()` coverage labels and FTN charting's `is_play_action`, 2023–2025: average EPA per dropback without and with play-action was 0.02 and 0.13 against COVER_4 (n = 4,835 and 888), 0.02 and 0.16 against COVER_3, and 0.01 and 0.13 against COVER_1. Play-action helps the offense against nearly every coverage by a similar margin.

[^rams]: Course calculation from nflverse `load_participation()` (NGS charting) joined to play-by-play `defteam`, 2020 regular season, dropbacks with a charted coverage (BLOWN and PREVENT excluded): Rams 41.8% COVER_3, 20.6% COVER_4, 15.5% COVER_6 and 15.0% COVER_1 (n = 548); 49ers 40.1% and Bears 37.3% quarters-plus-Cover 6; league 20.4%. The labels are post-snap; on the Rams' habit of "showing opposing quarterbacks one coverage before rotating into a different look right after," see Kaelen Jones, The Ringer (Jan. 13, 2021), cited in full in the note on Staley.

[^staley]: Kaelen Jones, "The Rams Defense Has L.A. on the Cusp of Another Deep Playoff Run," The Ringer (Jan. 13, 2021): https://theringer.com/2021/01/13/nfl/rams-defense-los-angeles-brandon-staley-aaron-donald-jalen-ramsey (Staley's years on Fangio's staffs in Chicago and Denver; Ramsey used outside and as the nickel or "star"; "much lighter boxes").

[^broncos]: Carolina Panthers, "Five things to know about new defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero" (Feb. 5, 2023): https://www.panthers.com/news/five-things-to-know-about-new-defensive-coordinator-ejiro-evero (2022 Broncos "seventh" in total defense at 320 yards a game and "third-best in net yards per passing attempt (5.6 – tied with Kansas City)"; five years with the Rams coaching safeties and the secondary, and their 2021 defensive passing game coordinator). Record: "2022 Denver Broncos season," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Denver_Broncos_season (5–12; head coach Nathaniel Hackett fired after a 4–11 start). 2026: Panthers.com, "With all 10 head coaching vacancies filled, Ejiro Evero set to return as defensive coordinator" (Feb. 1, 2026): https://www.panthers.com/news/with-all-10-head-coaching-vacancies-filled-ejiro-evero-set-to-return-defensive-coordinator .

[^surtain]: Denver Broncos, "Pat Surtain II named an AP first-team All-Pro; Justin Simmons selected to second team" (Jan. 2023): https://www.denverbroncos.com/news/pat-surtain-ii-named-an-ap-first-team-all-pro-justin-simmons-selected-to-second- . Coverage shares: course calculation as in the note on the 2020 Rams, 2022 season: Broncos 46.8% COVER_3, 15.6% COVER_4 and 17.7% COVER_6 (n = 603), sixth in the league in quarters-plus-Cover 6; league 24.8%; the Jets led at 45.5%.

[^dennard]: Michigan State Athletics, "Darqueze Dennard Wins Jim Thorpe Award" (Dec. 12, 2013): https://msuspartans.com/news/2013/12/12/Darqueze_Dennard_Wins_Jim_Thorpe_Award .

[^narduzzi-man]: FootballScoop account of Narduzzi's 2014 clinic talk, cited in full in the note on Roethlisberger: "Narduzzi admitted his coverage can look like man a lot of the time."
